--- title: "[SurvivalTree]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} A survival decision tree grown with the log-rank splitting rule. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_forest.py#L361-L712){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python SurvivalTree( *, max_depth=None, min_samples_split=6, min_samples_leaf=3, max_features=None, splitter="best", engine="numpy", random_state=None ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The tree recursively partitions subjects by covariate thresholds, at each step choosing the split that maximizes the two-sample log-rank statistic between the resulting child groups. Each leaf holds a Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard and a Kaplan-Meier survival curve estimated from its training subjects, evaluated on the full training set's event-time grid. Prediction routes a subject to a leaf and reads off that leaf's curves; the scalar risk score is the summed cumulative hazard (ensemble mortality). A single tree is a high-variance estimator and is most useful as an interpretable building block or the base learner of a `RandomSurvivalForest`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_depth]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum depth of the tree. `None` grows until other stopping rules apply. [min_samples_split]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[6]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum number of subjects a node must have to be eligible for splitting. [min_samples_leaf]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[3]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Minimum number of subjects required in each child of a split. [max_features]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of covariates considered at each split: `"sqrt"`, `"log2"`, an int, a float fraction, or `None` (all features). A random subset is drawn per node. [splitter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["best"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How thresholds are chosen: `"best"` (default) scans every candidate cut-point for the optimal log-rank split; `"random"` draws a single random threshold per candidate feature (the extremely-randomized-trees rule used by `ExtraSurvivalTrees`). [engine]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["numpy"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Compute backend for the best-split search: `"numpy"` (default) uses the deterministic vectorized path; `"numba"` uses a compiled kernel (requires the `fast` extra) that is faster on large datasets; `"auto"` uses Numba when available. The Numba path produces a statistically equivalent fit but, because it accumulates the log-rank statistic in a different order, may differ from the NumPy path in tie-breaking. [random_state]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Seed or `numpy.random.Generator` controlling the per-node feature subsampling. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Grow a survival tree on the bundled `lung` dataset and predict a risk score: ::: {#044b50ee .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="pandas").dropna(subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno"]) # Fit a survival tree and score the first five subjects tree = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit( "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog + ph.karno + wt.loss", data=lung ) tree.predict(lung)[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` array([34.84166667, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288]) ``` ::: ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
fit() Fit the survival tree to a right-censored response and covariate design.
predict() Predict a risk score, survival curves, or cumulative-hazard curves.
### [fit()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Fit the survival tree to a right-censored response and covariate design. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_forest.py#L451-L559){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python fit( surv, covariates=None, *, data=None, _rng=None, _event_times=None, _time=None, _event=None ) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [surv]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Surv | Outcome | str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A right-censored `Surv` response, built with `gw.Surv(time=..., event=...)`. An `Outcome` or a formula string such as `'Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age + sex'` is also accepted, with its columns read from `data`. The right-hand side sets `covariates`. [covariates]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A dataframe, a 2-D array, or a right-hand-side formula string evaluated against `data`. A list of column names in `data` also works. [data]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : A data frame (pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB, a lazy frame, ...) holding the columns named by the response and `covariates`. When `surv`{.gd-no-link} is an `Outcome` or a formula, rows with a missing value in any column used are dropped before fitting. Covariate formula strings and lists of column names are also resolved here. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [SurvivalTree]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The fitted estimator (for method chaining), with cached attributes such as `event_times_`, `n_features_in_`, and `feature_names_in_`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} Grow a survival tree on the `lung` dataset with a formula interface. The formula specifies both the response and the covariates in a single string: ::: {#df65f05a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="pandas").dropna( subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno"] ) tree = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit( "Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog + ph.karno", data=lung, ) tree ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` SurvivalTree (log-rank splits, 15 nodes, 8 leaves) n = 226, events = 163, features = 4 ``` ::: ::: The same fit can be done by passing an `Outcome` and the covariate columns separately: ::: {#b5a4809d .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2") tree2 = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit( death, covariates=["age", "sex", "ph.ecog", "ph.karno"], data=lung ) tree2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` SurvivalTree (log-rank splits, 15 nodes, 8 leaves) n = 226, events = 163, features = 4 ``` ::: ::: ### [predict()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Predict a risk score, survival curves, or cumulative-hazard curves. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_forest.py#L623-L697){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python predict(newdata=None, *, type="risk", times=None, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Three prediction types are available: 1. `type="risk"` (default): Ishwaran's ensemble mortality, the sum of the leaf cumulative hazard over the training event times. Higher values indicate higher risk. Returned as a 1-D NumPy array. 2. `type="survival"`: Kaplan-Meier survival probabilities $S(t \mid x)$ at `times`, one column per subject. Returned as a DataFrame. 3. `type="cumulative_hazard"`: Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard $H(t \mid x)$ at `times`. Returned as a DataFrame. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [newdata]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Covariates to predict for. `None` predicts for the training subjects. A data frame may also hold other columns. The covariates are picked out by name and coded as they were at fit time, so the frame the model was fit on can be passed as is. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["risk"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : One of `"risk"`, `"survival"`, or `"cumulative_hazard"`. [times]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Times at which to evaluate survival / cumulative hazard. Defaults to the training event times. Ignored for `type="risk"`. [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : DataFrame backend for curve output: `None`, `"pandas"`, `"polars"`, or `"pyarrow"`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [numpy.ndarray or DataFrame]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A risk vector, or a curve frame with a `time` column and one column per subject. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} Compute the ensemble-mortality risk score for each subject (a 1-D array where higher values indicate higher risk): ::: {#99fc605d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="pandas").dropna( subset=["ph.ecog", "ph.karno"] ) tree = gw.SurvivalTree(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit( "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + ph.ecog + ph.karno + wt.loss", data=lung ) tree.predict(lung)[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` array([34.84166667, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288, 95.15345288]) ``` ::: ::: Predict survival curves at specific time points. The result is a DataFrame with a `time` column and one column per subject: ::: {#ee736dc5 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree.predict(lung, type="survival", times=[180, 365, 730]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
